transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-10
Time: 16:00 - 17:15 PT
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood Solutions Eng); Sarah Kim (Vertex Head of ML), Tom Alvarez (Vertex Infra Lead), Priya Nair (Vertex Security)

Summary: Technical deep dive on on-prem / air-gapped deployment specifics - artifact delivery, offline licensing for GPU drivers, runtime perf (KV cache, continuous batching, quantization strategies). Action items captured at the end. Transcript follows; auto-transcript quality medium, occasional mis-hearings.

Topics: runtime perf, latency vs throughput, KV cache behavior, batching policies, quantization tradeoffs (int8/gptq/q4_0 etc), VPC/on-prem packaging, offline GPU driver licensing, artifact delivery mechanisms (signed tarball, USB, checksum, license token), rollback and fallback policies.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros? I'll hand off to Ravi for agenda.
[00:18] Ravi Patel: Hey all, Ravi from Redwood SE. Today we'll cover runtime perf fundamentals, KV cache patterns, how batching affects p99, and then move into on-prem specifics: artifact delivery, driver licensing in air-gapped env, and what we need from your side for a pilot.
[00:32] Sarah Kim: Sounds good. We're primarily concerned about latency at p95/p99 for chat use, and also the offline install constraints, like we cannot call out to license servers, no internet during install.
[00:45] Tom Alvarez: Yeah and we have tight security - we need checksums, signed artifacts, and the ability to vet the driver packages before applying to our nodes. Also we run NGC driver stack with specific kernel versions.
[00:59] Ravi Patel: Totally. We'll talk through offline transfer options (signed tarball + sha256, scp over an isolated bastion, USB delivery under chain-of-custody if required), and offline license tokens which are time-bound and can be consumed by our local license agent.
[01:18] Luis Ortega: Quick note: some customers prefer a signed RPM/DEB bundle for easier package management; others want a plain tar.gz with an installer script. Both are possible but we'll need kernel/driver compatibility info.
[01:33] Priya Nair: For security we need HSM/KMS compatibility mention - where keys live. If license tokens are generated, they must be signed by Redwood's key and validated locally; we can't send a call home.
[01:46] Maya Chen: We do support offline signed tokens and an offline license file. Our docs describe the token format, signed by our internal key, and we provide a verification tool that runs locally to validate signature against a public key bundle you load.
[02:00] Sarah Kim: Ok good. Now on perf: what's the expected tradeoff if we use int8 / GPTQ quantized models vs q4_0 or standard fp16? We care about quality delta for retrieval-augmented chat.
[02:15] Ravi Patel: Short answer: int8/GPTQ gives big memory savings and throughput boosts, but quality can degrade on some instruction-following tasks. q4_0/GPTQ variants depending on model often hit a sweet spot where throughput increases with modest quality drop. The runtime can select kernel pivots - choose INT8 matmuls vs fp16 - but model-specific evaluation recommended.
[02:36] Luis Ortega: Also quantization interacts with KV cache size - with smaller weights you can fit larger KV caches in GPU RAM which helps long-context chat throughput. But be careful: smaller quantized models can change the per-token compute profile.
[02:52] Tom Alvarez: How do you handle KV cache eviction? Our chat sessions can be long, 8-10k tokens. We don't want massive memory blowups.
[03:02] Ravi Patel: We keep the KV cache per-conversation and support both full KV and sharded KV strategies. For extremely long sessions we use prefix summarization + selective KV eviction; we also support offloading older KV segments to host RAM or NVMe with async prefetch. Offload introduces latency spikes on cache miss, so we recommend policy tuning and warmup strategies.
[03:26] Sarah Kim: Offloading to NVMe in air-gapped on-prem - do you support that? Network latency will be negligible but NVMe bandwidth is limited.
[03:36] Luis Ortega: Yes, on-prem customers often configure NVMe offload with prefetch windows. We recommend benchmarking with your sequence distribution because prefetch mis-prediction can cause p99 regressions.
[03:50] Priya Nair: From a security perspective, if offloading to disk, encryption at rest is mandatory for us. Do you support encrypted offload?
[03:58] Ravi Patel: Yes, we support encrypted local offload; customer can provide keys to the runtime or integrate with their KMS/HSM. For air-gapped installs we'd provide an integration path where you load the key material into the host HSM and the runtime binds to it.
[04:14] Tom Alvarez: Good. Now batching: we want to maximize throughput while keeping latency under 250ms for single-turn queries at p95. What batching strategy do you recommend?
[04:24] Ravi Patel: Continuous batching with dynamic batch sizing based on request queue and latency SLOs works well. The runtime does adaptive batching: it grows batch until either max batch size or batch timeout threshold. For low-latency SLOs, set batch timeout low (~5-10ms) and smaller max batch; for throughput-driven workloads raise timeouts and max batch size.
[04:44] Luis Ortega: There's also request-level prioritization - you can pin latency-sensitive traffic to a fast lane (dedicated GPUs or lower batch target) and route bulk/async prediction to a higher-throughput pool.
[04:55] Sarah Kim: Any numbers we can expect? For example, 8x A100 nodes, what's single-token latency and QPS for a 7B model in int8 vs fp16?
[05:07] Ravi Patel: Rough ballpark (very workload dependent): A single A100 can do ~120-180 tokens/sec for a 7B model in fp16 under real-world batching; in int8/GPTQ that can go up 1.8-2x. But end-to-end latency depends on prompt length, KV cache hits, and beam size. We'll run customers' profiles to produce realistic numbers.
[05:29] Tom Alvarez: We'll need those benchmark runs. We'll give you dataset and typical seq len distribution.
[05:36] Ravi Patel: Great. That ties into pilot scope. We'll run two sets: cold start (empty KV) and warm start scenarios with long contexts to see p50/p95/p99.
[05:48] Sarah Kim: About artifact delivery - what's in the on-prem package? Do you ship containers, binaries, or both? How do we update?
[05:57] Luis Ortega: We ship a set of artifacts: runtime binary (container image and an OCI tar), installer scripts, a signed driver bundle (if you want Redwood-provided driver), license file, and a verification script. For air-gapped installs we provide an artifacts manifest and sha256 checksums and a GPG-signed manifest. Updates are delivered as signed patch bundles; you can vet and apply them manually.
[06:20] Priya Nair: Who signs the artifacts? We need PKI chain info for our security team to verify signatures.
[06:26] Maya Chen: Artifacts are signed by Redwood's release key; we can provide the CA chain and public verification keys. If you require, we can do a customer-specific signing process or table stakes of SLSA provenance.
[06:39] Tom Alvarez: For GPU drivers - we often use vendor-provided drivers and have strict kernel matching. Do you require a specific driver, or can you run with our validated driver?
[06:50] Ravi Patel: We certify against a matrix of kernel + CUDA + NVIDIA driver versions. You can use your validated driver; we just need to confirm compatibility with the runtime and provide the matching CUDA/cuDNN libs. If you want Redwood to ship drivers, we'll deliver signed driver packages and a driver license file for offline activation.
[07:08] Sarah Kim: Driver license file? How does offline licensing for drivers work?
[07:13] Luis Ortega: For some NVIDIA enterprise drivers, there's a license/entitlement flow. For air-gapped customers, vendors sometimes allow an offline license file or token generated by vendor portal - Redwood supports consuming such files and providing a wrapper so everything is validated locally. For any vendor constraints we will coordinate with you and the vendor.
[07:33] Tom Alvarez: Are there legal constraints if you ship drivers? We need to run them through our legal review.
[07:38] Maya Chen: Understood. We can provide ABIs of packages and a list of files for legal to review, and we can also provide a process where you supply the driver and we package it into our installer.
[07:49] Priya Nair: On the license agent: does it run as a service that checks the offline token? Where's the key stored?
[07:56] Ravi Patel: The offline license agent is a local binary that validates the token signature and verifies expiry. The key material for signature verification is a public key you load once. Private keys remain with Redwood. For HSM customers we provide an integration path such that the private key is never required in the environment; only verification is done locally in a signed runtime.
[08:18] Sarah Kim: Ok thanks. Back to perf - can you explain kernel selection and how it adapts for sequence-length variance?
[08:25] Luis Ortega: The runtime has multiple kernel paths for attention and matmul; at compile time we prebuild kernels optimized for ranges of sequence lengths and batch sizes. At runtime we select the kernel based on the current request's effective sequence length distribution. There is a small recompilation cost for unusual shapes, but we cache compiled kernels. This is why workload histograms are important for optimal performance.
[08:48] Tom Alvarez: For our pilot we'll run varied seq lengths; what's the warmup requirement for kernel caches?
[08:55] Ravi Patel: Typical warmup is a few hundred tokens per shape; we'll include warmup scripts. For production you can precompute the hot shapes and keep them resident.
[09:06] Sarah Kim: Any recommendations on model version pinning vs autoswitching? We want to avoid regression surprises.
[09:13] Maya Chen: We recommend pinning model versions for production and using Redwood's canary rollout for experiments. For quantized variants we recommend evals on your prompt set and can integrate Redwood Optimize's eval harness. We'll also set up alerts on quality regressions.
[09:27] Priya Nair: Audit logs - we need proof of what was installed and when. Does the installer produce attestations?
[09:34] Luis Ortega: Yes, the installer outputs a signed install manifest listing artifact checksums, driver versions, and license token IDs, plus optional SLSA provenance.
[09:44] Tom Alvarez: Great. Let's capture next steps.
[09:48] Maya Chen: Action items we captured: Ravi will run perf bench with your workload; Tom to provide seq hist; Maya to send offline install + license checklist and signed artifact manifest example. Any other items?
[09:58] Sarah Kim: Please include a recommended config for NVMe offload thresholds and a suggested batching config for p95 under 250ms.
[10:06] Ravi Patel: Will do. Also include a note on quantization variants to test (fp16, q4_0, gptq-int8). We'll include a simple evaluation harness that runs your prompt set and reports quality delta.
[10:18] Tom Alvarez: Ok thanks everyone. End of call.

Auto-summary/closing notes: The team agreed to run an on-prem pilot with signed artifacts delivered offline. The customer will provide workload histograms and infra details; Redwood will provide benchmark results and an offline install + licensing checklist.

End transcript.
